newsitem.title: UK: Firm dollar pauses for breath at European close.
newsitem.headline: Firm dollar pauses for breath at European close.

text.p: The dollar closed higher, buoyed by mark weakness across the board, a Swiss franc slide following a surprise Swiss rate cut and by a rethink about U.S. interest rates.
Profit-taking and technical resistance in the mid-1.52 mark region took some of the foam off the dollar's rise but dealers said the U.S. unit is in fine fettle for more gains.

"The dollar looks well bid, helped by the weaker Swiss franc and the general softness of the mark," said Jeremy Stretch, currency strategist at NatWest Markets. "It has been hit by some profit-taking but there are buyers out there at lower levels."
Dealers said the next major hurdle for the dollar was now at 1.5250 marks where profit-taking set in earlier in the session.
The dollar got a helping hand from a half point cut in the Swiss discount rate to 1.0 percent. The move was in line with the recent decline in money market rates, the SNB said.
"The Swiss rate cut had quite a psychological impact on the dollar as it highlighted the dire economic situation in Europe," said Tony Norfield, treasury economist at ABN Amro in London.
The Swiss franc tumbled after the cut to a low of 1.2565 per dollar and 82.35 centimes from around 81.87 and 1.2425 just before the move. It settled at 82.28/31 and 1.2524/34 later.
The dollar was at 1.5225/35 marks and 110.42/48 yen at 1515 GMT versus 1.5115/20 and 110.36/46 at Wednesday's close here.
Norfield at ABN Amro said he expected the dollar to accelerate to the 1.54/1.55 mark area, provided U.S. yields did not drop more sharply.
"If that happened the dollar's yield premium would be diminishing which would put a question mark over its ability to rally much further in the longer term," said Norfield.
A surprisingly large drop in U.S. durable goods orders for August confirmed the view of some analysts that the Federal Reserve was right not to raise rates at this stage.

Others wondered whether the U.S. central bank will need to raise rates later this year. But since durable goods data are often subject to major revisions the dollar took the data in its stride and stayed afloat above 1.52 marks.

"The data suggest the economy is slowing and that it might be less likely that the Fed will raise rates if this continues," said Stretch at NatWest. "But durable goods are a notoriously volatile number, so I wouldn't get too hung about it."
Orders for durable goods fell 3.1 percent, the biggest monthly decline since April 1995. Economists had expected a slight drop of 0.1 percent from July.

In a briefing ahead of international finance meetings starting later this week in Washington U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said the U.S. economy was "very healthy" and that he saw no sign of inflation reigniting. He also reiterated his support for a strong dollar.
Sterling extended its gains against the mark, helped by the firmer dollar/mark. Analysts said the comparatively high real yields on UK gilts remained a major sterling positive.
The pound was close to session highs at 2.3778/83 marks, up from 2.3635/40. The next key hurdle is the pound's 1996 high at 2.3822.-- Astrid Zweynert London newsroom + 44 171 542 7792
